newsitem.title: ITALY: We're unpopular but we work, Italy's Prodi says.
newsitem.headline: We're unpopular but we work, Italy's Prodi says.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi acknowledged on Wednesday that his centre-left government was unpopular but said it was succeeding in improving Italy's economic performance in order to achieve its key goal -- Europe.
"It's a policy of action that has to have absolute priority in moments like this -- even if it costs," Prodi wrote in a front-page letter to La Stampa newspaper.
"...it's a price we're paying constantly in terms of unpopularity," he added.

Prodi, a former businessman and economics professor seen as a colourless political novice before his Olive Tree coalition won power last April, was replying to an editorial on Monday which called him a "government manager", not a political leader.

Prodi, who has come under fire this week from members of his own coalition, has always cultivated a low-key image in contrast to the flamboyance of opposition centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi. He said he did not find the description insulting.
Italy was facing a "very delicate moment...and I think manageriality is an indispensable extra value at present".

He said Italians who voted for him, giving the left its first taste of power for nearly 50 years, had known big changes lay ahead and he trumpeted the achievements of his 10-month-old government -- already older than many of its predecessors.

He noted "the significant turnaround in economic indicators which show that our policies are giving good results...that will allow the country not only to enter Europe but above all to enter it in good health and to stay there".
Prodi has staked his political credibility on making Italy a founder member of Europe's single currency at its start in 1999 and has pushed through unpopular tax hikes and spending cuts.
He has presided over a fall in inflation to lows not seen for more than a quarter of a century and interest rate falls.

An austerity budget heavy in new taxes to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($36.7 billion) off the 1997 deficit was intended to ensure Italy met a key economic and monetary union goal of curbing the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.
But a spending overshoot spoiled his sums and he is planning to unveil another mini-budget shortly to achieve the EMU target.
Prodi is due to meet coalition parties and key allies, including hard-left Communist Refoundation party and Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini's Italian Renewal party, on Thursday.
